detail.abstract: Research suggests applying Artificial intelligence (AI) for agile projects results in risk identification, backlog management, sprint planning and resource allocation. Yet organizations that provided a generative AI license to every member of a delivery team are not delivering software faster. This paper explores the reason for this problem. The shortfall does not come from the models. It follows from how the tools were introduced.,Firms hand generative AI to developers, testers, architects, product owners and scrum masters, who use it as a personal assistant thereby capping the capability. The analysis behind delivery decisions migrates into private conversations that no reviewer can inspect. Further, when a generative tool is used continuously across many small steps, the tool builds a stable working memory of the project and returns well-referenced material. Once the application is live and a defect appears, the tool cannot reliably diagnose work its own reasoning produced, and blame attaches to a tool.,To address these issues, we propose AI software factory: a production line of role-specific Agents, designed and commissioned before use, inspected at defined points, and reviewed by qualified humans at the sprint boundary rather than at every handoff. Agents are written by expert prompt engineers, reviewers judge outputs, and their findings return to the Agent’s author as versioned engineering change.

detail.abstract: Molten salt thermal energy storage (TES) coupled with coal-fired power units is regarded as one of the most promising routes for deep peak-shaving retrofits. Among the available heat-discharge options, using molten salt to replace the regenerative extraction steam for feedwater heating offers the simplest configuration and the lowest retrofit cost. Existing studies, however, predominantly rely on steady-state platforms or system-level lumped-parameter simulations, and therefore fail to resolve the transient heat transfer inside the heat exchanger, which is in fact the dominant bottleneck restricting the load ramp rate. This paper establishes a dynamic model of the load response in this mode for a 660 MW supercritical unit. The high-pressure feedwater heater (HPH) is modelled as three zones, with Nusselt film condensation corrected for tube rows on the shell side, a piecewise Nusselt correlation covering the laminar, transition and turbulent regimes on the tube side, and a dimensionless correction referenced to the rated heat balance for the migration of fluid properties. A nine-stage-group turbine model based on the Flügel formula turns the redistribution of extraction steam into the power output. The feedwater flow rate is stepped down to 0 % (full bypass), 30 %, 50 % and 80 % of the design value at 30 %, 50 % and 75 % turbine heat acceptance (THA). Both the mean feedwater temperature and the shell-side pressure then rise without overshoot along an approximately first-order path, and the settling time is set by the tube-side water inventory rather than by the heat storage of the tube-bundle metal. The settling time shortens as the unit load rises. The maximum load increment reaches 16.4 MW (2.5 %Pe), 32.2 MW (4.9 %Pe) and 58.8 MW (8.9 %Pe) at 30 %, 50 % and 75 % THA, respectively, and the corresponding standard average ramp rate over the 10 %–90 % steady-state band is 1.95, 5.58 and 15.8 %Pe/min. The results provide a basis for designing and controlling such retrofits.

detail.title: Market-Based Carbon Responsibility Accounting for Electricity Contracts and Green Certificate Transfers
detail.abstract: The coexistence of bundled renewable electricity, attribute-stripped electricity, fossil-based contracts, and stand-alone green certificates complicates the allocation of market-based carbon responsibility. Environmental attributes may be claimed more than once, while responsibility deducted from certificate buyers may lack an explicit recipient, creating inconsistent accounting boundaries. This study proposes a closed-loop framework that coordinates electricity contracts with environmental-attribute ownership and transfer. Settlement priority ensures that each attribute is used once, source records link certificates to corresponding attribute-stripped electricity, and entity-level responsibility is updated after certificate settlement. Responsibility associated with a matched certificate is assigned to the relevant contract user; otherwise, it is distributed among consumers of the unmatched electricity through residual allocation. The framework distinguishes physical emissions from market-based responsibility while preserving system-wide accounting consistency. Comparative cases clarify the functions of settlement priority, source matching, and residual allocation under intertemporal settlement, renewable-generation variations, and partial delivery defaults. The results show that the procedure can identify responsibility omissions and duplicate attribute claims under the specified settings. The framework provides a transparent accounting approach for electricity markets where bundled contracts and independently traded environmental attributes coexist.

title: On Multi-entity, Multivariate Quickest Change Point Detection

detail.title: On Multi-entity, Multivariate Quickest Change Point Detection

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: We propose an unsupervised learning framework for online quickest Change Point Detection (qCPD) for multi-entity, multivariate time series data, a problem setting in which system-level behavioral shifts must be detected across a population of interacting entities whose number and behavior may be uncertain or evolve. This setting, motivated by applications such as crowd monitoring where traditional sensing methods (e.g., video surveillance) may be infeasible, is not addressed by existing single-stream CPD methods or multi-entity anomaly detection techniques. We introduce IDfN-to-SWAS, a two-stage detection pipeline in which entity-level deviations from nominal behavior, Individual Deviation from Normality (IDfN) scores, are aggregated into a System-Wide Anomaly Score (SWAS). A CUSUM-based sequential detector is applied to the SWAS to identify persistent or abrupt system-level changes with low detection delay. The framework requires only training data obtained under normal system operation to determine the model required for IDfN calculation. Importantly, it naturally supports variable entity counts without retraining and is compatible with a wide range of anomaly scoring backbones. Evaluations on synthetic datasets and crowd simulations, explicitly designed for anomaly detection in group behaviors, demonstrate that our method accurately detects system-level changes, offering a scalable and privacy-preserving solution for monitoring complex multi-entity systems. To support reproducible benchmarking in this emerging problem domain, we additionally release three first-of-their-kind multi-entity multivariate datasets explicitly designed for evaluating system-level CPD in interactive multi-entity systems.

title: An integrated network–agent simulation framework for railway marshalling yard operations based on a bi-level yard network
affiliations: Southwest Jiaotong University, Southwest Jiaotong University, Southwest Jiaotong University - School of Transportation and Logistics, Southwest Jiaotong University and Southwest Jiaotong University

detail.title: An integrated network–agent simulation framework for railway marshalling yard operations based on a bi-level yard network

affiliations.org_name: Southwest Jiaotong University - School of Transportation and Logistics

detail.abstract: High-fidelity simulation is essential for analyzing the tightly coupled and multi-stage operations of railway marshalling yards, as it can reproduce dynamic system behaviors and thereby support accurate capacity assessment, bottleneck identification, and operational plan simulation. Existing approaches, however, often have difficulty representing both yard infrastructure and operational logic while reproducing complete operational processes. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an integrated network–agent simulation framework (INASF) for marshalling yard operations based on a bi-level yard network (BLYN). The region network encodes operationally feasible transitions among functional regions, whereas the facility network represents the physical connectivity of tracks and switches. Train, locomotive, and railcar agents are established to represent the state transitions and operational interactions. A bi-level routing mechanism converts each region-level path into executable facility-level routes, while an occupancy decision coordinates route locking, final facility feasibility checks, and resource release. Together, these components reproduce train arrival, disassembly, accumulation, make-up, and departure processes. A full-scale (1:1) simulation model of Wuhan North Marshalling Yard is developed, and its downstream subsystem is selected as the simulation scenario for experimental evaluation. Routing verification shows that the prescribed movement sequences and physical connectivity are maintained in the examined cases, while differences between simulated and field-observed mean total processing times range from 3.3\% to 6.9\%. The estimated integrated train handling capacity of the modeled downstream subsystem is approximately 257 trains/24 h. With 50 railcars per train, this corresponds to approximately 12,850 railcars/24 h, differing by 2.6\% from the field-observed average daily handling volume under the same counting convention. Utilization analysis under the 10 min/train scenario identifies the hump subsystem as the primary bottleneck in inbound processing. These results demonstrate the framework’s utility for executable yard operation simulation, capacity evaluation, and bottleneck identification. An executable system based on INASF has been in formal operational use at Wuhan North Marshalling Yard since 2025, supporting capacity assessment, operating plan simulation, and potential bottleneck identification.

title: A Staged Model for Trust in Agri-Food Blockchain Ecosystems: Extending Value-Sensitive Design with Contingency Theory
affiliations: University of Waikato, University of Canterbury and University of Canterbury

detail.title: A Staged Model for Trust in Agri-Food Blockchain Ecosystems: Extending Value-Sensitive Design with Contingency Theory
detail.abstract: Blockchain technology has been proposed as a means of strengthening trust and transparency across agri-food supply chains (ASCs), in which numerous loosely connected stakeholders must collaborate to move products from farm to consumer. Adoption nevertheless remains uneven, in part because the dominant frameworks for understanding stakeholder acceptance, including Value-Sensitive Design (VSD), tend to treat values as stable properties tied to a stakeholder's organizational role. This paper challenges that assumption. Using Q-methodology, agri-food industry experts were surveyed across four ASC scenarios (production, processing and packaging, distribution and warehousing, and retailing) to map the subjective structure of stakeholder priorities toward blockchain-enabled trust and value. Factor analysis identified 12 distinct practitioner archetypes across the four core supply chain stages, and a Sankey diagram tracing individual exemplars across scenarios shows that the same participant frequently shifts between priority archetypes as their position in the supply chain changes. These findings extend VSD from a role-based model to a stage-sensitive one: stakeholder values are not fixed traits of a role but are activated by context. The paper interprets this pattern through a contingency lens. Rather than assuming that blockchain and Internet of Things (IoT) capabilities are universally beneficial, their value depends on the fit between the technology configuration and the specific stage-level and stakeholder-level conditions in which it is deployed. The paper offers a structured typology to guide blockchain system design, providing software architects, business leaders, and regulators with practical guidance for building adaptive, stage-aware architectures rather than uniform, one-size-fits-all systems.

title: Graph Convolutional and Multi-cale Convolutional Network for Tool Wear Prediction in CNC Milling
affiliations: Shandong Jianzhu University, Qilu Institute of Technology and Shandong University

detail.title: Graph Convolutional and Multi-cale Convolutional Network for Tool Wear Prediction in CNC Milling
detail.abstract: Accurate tool wear prediction is critical for improving machining quality and reducing production downtime in modern manufacturing systems. However,existing data-driven approaches often fail to effectively model inter-sensor correlations and multi-scale temporal characteristics simultaneously, which limits prediction accuracy in complex machining environments. To address this issue,this paper proposes a graph convolutional network multi-scale convolutional neural network (GCN-MSCNN) for tool wear prediction based on multi-sensor data.In the proposed method, force, torque, vibration, and acoustic signals are first processed to extract time- and frequency-domain features. A graph convolutional network (GCN) is employed to model correlations among different sensors, while a multi-scale convolutional neural network (MSCNN) is used to capture degradation features at multiple temporal resolutions. The learned relational and multi-scale features are fused to achieve accurate wear prediction.The proposed model is evaluated on the public PHM 2010 datasets and a real-world QIT-CEMC datasets collected under practical machining conditions. Experimental results show that GCN-MSCNN consistently outperforms representative machine learning and deep learning models. On PHM 2010, the proposed method achieves RMSE values as low as 4.59 and 5.45, significantly reducing prediction errors compared with LSTM-based approaches. On QIT CEMC, the model achieves the best performance under full multi-sensor fusion (RMSE = 3.54, MAE = 2.24), demonstrating its effectiveness in handling heterogeneous sensor information and complex operating conditions.The results indicate that the proposed GCN-MSCNN provides an effective solution for multi-sensor tool wear prediction in advanced manufacturing environments.

title: Human capital disclosure in words and photographs: Evidence from Japan
affiliations: Fukuoka University and Kyushu University

detail.title: Human capital disclosure in words and photographs: Evidence from Japan
detail.abstract: We examine how firms’ stated emphasis on employees corresponds to the use of employee photographs in integrated reports. Our sample comprises 3,377 reports from 546 Japanese listed firms for 2016–2024. We apply large language models to select employee photographs and assess whether they accompany accounts of employees’ experiences or participation in specific activities. Stronger people orientation, measured from annual securities reports, is associated with more extensive photograph use and more photographs per page accompanying such descriptions. Moreover, the association with photograph quantity is more pronounced when human capital narratives are more readable. These findings suggest that firms’ stated attitudes toward employees extend beyond written narratives to their visual presentation of human capital through employees’ images and experiences.

title: From Player Content to Feasible Game Add-Ons,A traceable decision-support case study of Cities: Skylines
affiliations: Chongqing Technology and Business University

detail.title: From Player Content to Feasible Game Add-Ons,A traceable decision-support case study of Cities: Skylines
detail.abstract: Player-generated reviews and mods offer abundant evidence for game development, but they do not directly identify add-on projects that fit a studio's resource mix. This study develops a traceable decision-support case that links public player content to scoped deliverables, role-specific work packages and constrained portfolio choice. Using 7,693 English- and Chinese-language reviews from 41 official expansions and creator packs and 263 sampled player-created items for Cities: Skylines, we construct lexical review signals and alternative mod-supply compositions for buildings, transport and maps. Three candidate add-on specifications are then evaluated under budget, art, engineering and testing limits. Under the declared planning assumptions, buildings plus a map is the highest-scoring feasible portfolio at the broad direction level. Once the same directions are translated into explicit work packages, that combination becomes infeasible because of art and testing requirements, and a compact transport project is selected before any cost revision. Sensitivity and interval analyses identify the input, incremental-value, workload and omitted-cost boundaries that reverse or invalidate the choice. The study contributes a transparent bridge from player-generated evidence to feasible development decisions, while keeping demand, production assumptions and commercial outcomes conceptually separate.

title: The Certainty Paradox in Leadership: Adaptive Thinking and Demands for Clarity Under Uncertainty
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University

detail.title: The Certainty Paradox in Leadership: Adaptive Thinking and Demands for Clarity Under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Leaders are expected to provide direction in situations that are not yet fully understood. This creates a recurring tension: effective judgement may require openness to competing interpretations, incomplete evidence and changing conditions, while leadership roles demand decisiveness and clarity. This paper develops the certainty paradox to describe the tension between interpretive openness and sufficient closure for coordinated action. Drawing on paradox theory, organisational sensemaking and research on epistemic motivation and cognitive closure, it argues that the leadership problem is not uncertainty itself or the requirement for clarity, but the possibility that demands for resolution end interpretive work too early. Premature epistemic closure is introduced to describe this process.The empirical study draws on survey data from 61 managers, directors, executives and founders within a broader sample of 102 professionals. Most respondents reported engaging with competing perspectives: 93.4% recognised oversimplified either/or choices, 91.8% considered competing perspectives before decisions, and 86.9% believed stronger decisions can emerge from exploring between alternatives. However, 78.7% reported being expected to provide clear answers under ambiguity, while only 41.0% felt their environment supported taking time to think through complexity. Adaptive thinking was positively associated with environments valuing nuanced thinking (r = .50, p < .001), whereas expectations for clarity were not significantly related to adaptive thinking (r = .14, p = .296).The findings position leadership under uncertainty as a problem of moving between openness and commitment, distinguishing demands for clarity from premature epistemic closure and locating adaptive judgement within the interaction between leader cognition and context.

title: Virtual Machine Consolidation in Cloud Computing Using Prophet's Forecasting Tool
affiliations: University of Lleida, University of Lleida, University of Lleida, University of Lleida, University of Lleida, University of Lleida, University of Lleida and University of Lleida

detail.title: Virtual Machine Consolidation in Cloud Computing Using Prophet's Forecasting Tool
detail.abstract: Cloud computing through the use of Virtual Machines (VMs) allows data center providers to modulate the computing resources allocated to users based on their needs. This assignment must satisfy user service level requirements (SLA) while reducing datacenter costs by maximizing resource usage and minimizing energy consumption. One powerful tool is the ability to redistribute the host load by reallocating the VMs that collapse the hosts. However, the migration process should be done cautiously, as the new VM allocation can negatively affect the VMs present in the target hosts, inciting unexpected new migrations. Furthermore, migrations are not free of charge as they require extra energy consumption and can also overload the interconnection network. This paper evaluates the effectiveness of combining Prophet forecasting and Bollinger Bands to predict cloud workloads, leveraging trend and seasonality analysis to improve virtual machine consolidation. To address this challenge, we propose a mechanism that prioritizes the migration of the most significant virtual machines according to their impact on host communications and energy consumption, together with a more realistic assessment of the impact of communications on overall power usage. The proposed approach was evaluated through an extensive analysis using cloud workloads from multiple providers (PlanetLab, Alibaba, Materna and Microsoft Azure) and compared against recent methods in the literature with similar optimization objectives. The results indicate that the proposed approach constitutes an effective and robust method for decision-making in VM migration processes across workloads in cloud computing environments.

title: Probabilistic multi-horizon forecasting and early warning of low residual chlorine in district metered areas using conformal prediction and explainable artificial intelligence
affiliations: Incheon National University

detail.title: Probabilistic multi-horizon forecasting and early warning of low residual chlorine in district metered areas using conformal prediction and explainable artificial intelligence
detail.abstract: Maintaining an adequate disinfectant residual throughout drinking water distribution networks is a central task of water quality management, and forecasts of residual chlorine in district metered areas (DMAs) would allow utilities to anticipate low-residual conditions rather than react to them. This study develops and evaluates a probabilistic early-warning framework for DMA-scale chlorine using one year of hourly residual chlorine, electrical conductivity, turbidity, and water temperature observations from five DMAs in Incheon, Republic of Korea. Eight forecasting approaches, from naive baselines through ridge regression and tree ensembles to recurrent and Transformer networks, were first benchmarked at lead times of 1 to 24 h under a chronological protocol; split-conformal prediction was then applied to the best model to produce calibrated forecast intervals and exceedance probabilities for a block-specific low-residual threshold, and the framework was stress-tested with a rolling four-fold seasonal cross-validation and a leave-one-block-out transfer experiment. Forecast skill relative to persistence was concentrated at lead times of 3–12 h and was largest, 27–29%, in the summer fold, when elevated water temperature accelerates chlorine decay. The conformal intervals attained 89.1% empirical coverage against a nominal 90%, and the derived low-residual warnings reached ROC-AUC values of 0.98 at 1 h and 0.91 at 24 h; warning skill persisted under absolute action thresholds of 0.3–0.4 mg/L. Ridge regression was statistically indistinguishable from the best deep models at all horizons, and its advantage widened when training data were scarce; models transferred to an entirely unseen block with accuracy losses below 6%. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses showed that forecasts rest almost entirely on chlorine self-history and the diurnal cycle, and that the learned temperature effect is negative and strengthens with lead time, in agreement with decay kinetics. The framework provides calibrated, transferable low-residual warnings from data that utilities already archive.

title: Mapping challenges and needs to support fire management in The Netherlands and Belgium
affiliations: Wageningen University & Research, Wageningen University, Wageningen University, Ghent University and Wageningen University & Research

detail.title: Mapping challenges and needs to support fire management in The Netherlands and Belgium
detail.abstract: As fire regimes are expanding, wildfires are becoming an increasing challenge in temperate countries where fire science and management is growing but still is in its infancy. Using a mixed methods approach combining a survey with policy workshops for professional stakeholders in The Netherlands and Belgium (n=107 and n=60 respondents, respectively), we mapped their perception of challenges, ideas for solutions, as well as their needs for knowledge, skills and data. Results show a small but sizeable and mostly part-time fire community, with 80% of respondents working on wildfire for ≤30% of their time. Respondents are critical of their country’s preparedness for the fires of today and the future, and identified five key challenges for fire management in their countries: lack of expertise and knowledge, financial means and personnel, urgency and (political) priority, collaboration and coordination, and rules and responsibilities. The key solutions proposed are to foster collaboration, and creating a central organization for coordination and knowledge sharing, national frameworks and guidelines, area-specific fire management plans, and funding and support. Knowledge, skills and data required to address these challenges and solutions are technical, analytical, governance, communication, interpersonal, networks and knowledge sharing. To strengthen the resilience of ecosystems and society for the fires of today and those of the future, landscape fires must be embedded in educational and training curricula across emerging fire regions, to support capacity building of its growing fire community and help expansion of its workforce that this domain urgently needs.

detail.abstract: Solar power is becoming the largest source of new electricity, and batteries are following it to shift midday output into the evening peak. However, a battery fixed where solar output is seasonal stays idle for months, and every idle day raises its cost of storage. This paper proposes installing containerized lithium iron phosphate batteries on a converted bulk carrier that moves between regions with opposite solar seasons. The arrangement was named battery energy storage system ship (BESS ship). A BESS ship consists of battery containers, power conversion equipment and a shore connection to a port substation. The ship charges from surplus solar power, then discharges into the evening peak. When the season changes, the ship sails to the other region with higher demand for storage. A static 1 GW, 4 GWh battery in southern Brazil that cycles only in summer stores energy at 275 USD/MWh, with battery degradation. A BESS ship that cycles in the South in summer and the Northeast in winter is estimated at 162 to 192 USD/MWh. The ship stays cheaper unless the static battery also cycles on more than 85 to 140 winter days. The relocation trip uses 17% to 40% of a full charge, so the ship can sail on its own battery. One ship equals 1% of the 108 GW of battery storage added worldwide in 2025. BESS ships could be an affordable alternative to static batteries where solar surplus moves between regions with the seasons.

title: Bridging the Global–Regional Implementation Gap in Coastal Sustainability: A CrossScale Diagnostic and Network Governance Framework
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Southern Cross University, Southern Cross University, University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, University of South Carolina and University of South Carolina

detail.title: Bridging the Global–Regional Implementation Gap in Coastal Sustainability: A CrossScale Diagnostic and Network Governance Framework

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science

detail.abstract: Coastal sustainability is a widely recognized global goal, yet progress on the ground remains uneven across regions. This study develops a cross-scale diagnostic framework to explain this persistent gap by combining two complementary datasets: a global survey of individual perceptions around global priorities for coastal sustainability (N = 214, 79 countries) using a regional institutional census of participating organizations in a regional coastal sustainability meta-network across East and Southeast Asia (N=18 organisations), examining participants' perceptions of the enabling conditions required to achieve aligned coastal sustainability goals through joint activities. We interpret the ”global–regional implementation gap” as a form of relational decoupling — a structural mismatch between globally stated priorities and regionally available enabling conditions. Our results show that governance is consistently ranked as the top global priority, whereas regional partner organizations report binding constraints in funding (100% of respondents), policy fragmentation (58.8%), and duplication of effort (41.2%). Social Network Analysis revealed a fragmented network structure. Although Meta-Network partner organisations maintain, or aspire to maintain, strong collaborative relationships with organisations external to the Meta-Network, no existing or desired collaborative ties were identified among partner organisations themselves. This limited internal connectivity suggests constrained capacity for collective action and knowledge exchange within the Meta-Network. In response, we propose an Iterative Network Architecture designed to foster stronger collaborative ties and enable collective action, combining thematic clusters with regional hubs, linked through blended funding and rotating governance. Building on knowledge-to-action scholarship, we argue that the binding constraint on coastal sustainability in this setting is not a lack of information, and cannot be explained solely by resource availability, but rather the absence of relational infrastructure to support interorganizational collaboration. Our analysis therefore highlights relational capacity—the structures, processes and incentives that enable actors to coordinate, exchange knowledge and act collectively—as a critical missing component in translating shared sustainability priorities into coordinated action. The proposed architecture is designed to address this gap through mechanisms for strengthening connectivity, enabling brokerage, and reshaping coordination incentives across the network.

title: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing:  Evidence from the Space Race
affiliations: University of Calgary, Florida State University, University of Calgary and Duke University - Fuqua School of Business

detail.title: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing:  Evidence from the Space Race

affiliations.org_name: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business

detail.abstract: This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for USmanufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented publicinvestment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA’s Space Race investments across industriesand locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures ofautomation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically moreautomation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistentdeclines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications. In contrast, we find little evidence of systematic changesin skill composition. These findings show that mission-oriented public R&D can shape the direction of technological change and have lasting distributional consequences.

title: Training-Induced Variability in Low-Timestep Accuracy: A Multi-Seed Evaluation of Confidence-Threshold Stopping in Spiking Neural Networks
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Training-Induced Variability in Low-Timestep Accuracy: A Multi-Seed Evaluation of Confidence-Threshold Stopping in Spiking Neural Networks

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) can reduce the cost of neural computation by exploiting sparse, event-driven synaptic operations, but the energy cost of rate-coded inference increases with the number of simulation timesteps, motivating input-adaptive confidence-threshold stopping policies that terminate computation once sufficient evidence has accumulated. Such policies are typically validated using a single trained checkpoint. This study asks whether that is sufficient, using a directly trained convolutional SNN (824,458 parameters) on Fashion-MNIST, evaluated across five independently trained checkpoints that differ only in random seed (weight initialization, data shuffling, and train/validation split), with an identical architecture, training protocol, and patience-based early-stopping criterion for every seed.,The primary finding is that accuracy at low fixed timestep budgets is highly sensitive to which of the five seeds produced the checkpoint, while accuracy at high timestep budgets and under the adaptive policy is not. At a fixed budget of T = 4, accuracy ranged from 22.85% to 48.50% across seeds (mean 37.87%, SD 9.71 percentage points). At T = 64, the range was 88.97–90.41% (SD 0.57 points), and under the validation-selected adaptive stopping policy (confidence threshold θ = 0.80, held fixed across all seeds) it was 88.97–90.45% (SD 0.58 points) — roughly a 17-fold reduction in cross-seed variability from T = 4 to T = 64. This variability correlated strongly with how many epochs each seed's training required to reach its early-stopping plateau (Pearson r = 0.95, p = 0.014, n = 5): checkpoints that trained longer before plateauing had systematically higher low-timestep accuracy, and this was not merely a proportional effect of general checkpoint quality — the accuracy gap between T = 64 and T = 4 itself shrank significantly with more pre-plateau training (r = -0.95, p = 0.013). This directly contradicts a training-objective-based hypothesis proposed after only two non-matched training attempts in an earlier version of this study; that hypothesis is rejected by the controlled multi-seed data reported here.,Despite this low-timestep fragility, the adaptive stopping policy itself was robust across all five seeds: paired McNemar tests showed adaptive inference significantly more accurate than fixed T = 32 in every seed (all p < 10⁻⁴) and statistically indistinguishable from fixed T = 64 in every seed (all p ≥ 0.39), with a mean energy reduction of 59.96% (SD 4.41 points) relative to fixed T = 64 and a smaller, more variable 17.65% (SD 8.86 points) relative to fixed T = 32. The practical implication is that reporting a confidence-threshold adaptive-SNN result from a single trained checkpoint risks presenting an artifact of that specific training run — particularly for any claim involving low-timestep fixed-budget accuracy — and multi-seed evaluation should be treated as a minimum standard for this class of result, not an optional robustness check.

title: Crossing sectors, reconfiguring ties: Academic mobility and collaboration networks
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics and School of Economics, Huazhong University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Crossing sectors, reconfiguring ties: Academic mobility and collaboration networks

affiliations.org_name: Central University of Finance and Economics
Huazhong University of Science and Technology - School of Economics

detail.abstract: Researcher mobility is often expected to connect academic knowledge with practice, but entering a new sector need not preserve the relationships that make such connections possible. We develop an account of collaboration reconfiguration that distinguishes changes in partner composition, tie substitution, and collaboration among a mover’s contacts. Using 202,002 economics and policy publications from 2000–2025, we identify 1,045 academic-to-nonacademic transitions and compare these researchers with academics who change universities. The estimated change in nonacademic coauthor share is 0.176 in the full matched sample and 0.215 among 31 employment-verified movers. Both estimates indicate an economically meaningful shift in the sectoral composition of subsequent coauthorship. In a separate mover-only decomposition, collaborators outside the destination institution account for approximately 39% of the mover-level change. Descriptive tie summaries show substantial partner turnover alongside the formation of new collaborations. Academic and nonacademic contacts linked through movers also collaborate subsequently without the mover in a subset of cases. Among returners, nonacademic coauthor share declines after re-entry into academia. The study distinguishes access to nonacademic partners from sustained integration between research communities. It suggests that mobility evaluations should examine which relationships are created, displaced, and sustained, alongside conventional measures of individual research performance.

title: A Geometric Bayesian Parameter Inference Method for Structurally Non-identifiable Models
affiliations: University of Alberta, University of Alberta and University of Alberta

detail.title: A Geometric Bayesian Parameter Inference Method for Structurally Non-identifiable Models
detail.abstract: We consider parameter inference for ordinary differential equation (ODE) models with structural non-identifiability. Such models arise in a wide range of scientific fields, including control theory, systems biology, and public health. Structural non-identifiability occurs when distinct parameter values produce identical model outputs, resulting in lower-dimensional manifolds of observationally equivalent parameter values in the parameter space. This presents challenges for Bayesian inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, often leading to poor mixing and slow convergence.We develop a geometric MCMC method that uses information from structural identifiability analysis. The proposed Identifiability-Aware Geometric MCMC constructs proposals that moves along and across non-identifiable manifolds. We show that the proposed method targets the correct posterior distribution and is ergodic under standard regularity conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the method can improve sampling efficiency and convergence compared with conventional MCMC methods for structurally non-identifiable models.

title: Everyday Cash Usage and Perceived Corruption: Evidence for Developed Countries
affiliations: Institute of Economics, Polish Academy of Sciences, Warsaw School of Economics (SGH), Nicolas Copernicus University in Torun and Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) - Applied Economics Department

detail.title: Everyday Cash Usage and Perceived Corruption: Evidence for Developed Countries

affiliations.org_name: Institute of Economics, Polish Academy of Sciences
Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) - Applied Economics Department

detail.abstract: From July 2027, the European Union will cap cash payments for goods and services at EUR 10,000, on the premise that traceable payments make corruption and other illicit activity harder to conceal. We test this hypothesis using a new database that compiles payment diary studies into a measure of the share of consumer transactions settled in cash, covering 29 high-income countries over 2012--2025. Across countries, higher cash usage is robustly associated with higher perceived corruption after controlling for GDP per capita: a ten-percentage-point higher cash share goes with a 3.0-point higher score on the inverted Corruption Perceptions Index. The association holds for three composite corruption indices, for each of the eight source scores underlying the index, and for volume- and value-based measures of cash usage. Within countries, by contrast, we find no evidence that changes in cash usage precede changes in perceived corruption, or vice versa. This implies that the identified cross-country pattern appears structural rather than mechanical: policies that reduce cash usage may complement broader anti-corruption efforts, but should not be expected to reduce perceived corruption quickly.

title: Self-calibrating forecasting of construction time in drill-and-blast tunnels: starting from the rounds already executed

detail.abstract: Monte Carlo simulation forecasts the construction time of a drill-and-blast drive far more accurately than deterministic planning, but it first requires a probability distribution fitted to each unit operation of the cycle, which in the case studied here took three months of continuous timing. That data requirement, and not the mathematics, is what has prevented wider adoption. This paper reverses the order: the forecast is issued with whatever rounds have already been excavated, ten being enough, and is re-estimated as the face advances, so that the works themselves become the data source. Durations are simulated by Gaussian anamorphosis over the available sample, without postulating parametric distributions, and the uncertainty of that sample is propagated by bootstrap resampling. Three results follow. The shift mechanism is invariant with respect to the duration distributions, at 506.8 effective minutes per shift, which yields an analytical predictor accurate to 0.5%. Conventional simulation fed with ten rounds declares only 8% of the variance its own forecast carries, and its 90% interval does not contain the true construction time. Enlarging that sample with simulated rather than measured rounds conveys no information. With rounds measured on site, convergence is systematic and the forecast is centred in every replicate by 182 m of advance, under one third of the drive.

detail.abstract: We revisit the case of Grameen Bank to reassess the lessons this microfinance pioneer offers about sustaining inclusive business models. Grameen’s legacy extends beyond its Nobel Prize-winning role in establishing microfinance: its evolving business model has survived the test of time while many of its replicators have not. An evolutionary perspective on business model innovation guides our evaluation of three explanations for Grameen’s renewed growth over the last two decades: continuity in its founding model, mission drift toward commercial priorities, and architectural business model innovation. Combining insider accounts with four decades of financial and operational data, we find the strongest support for architectural innovation. Grameen’s leaders discovered an unexpectedly deep market for microsavings and made local deposits central to financing microcredit and branch expansion, reducing dependence on external capital. Our findings connect research on microcredit with broader financial inclusion by explaining how Grameen’s leaders came to view savings and lending as complementary components of an inclusive banking model. More broadly, we show how architectural innovation changes the lessons scholars and practitioners draw from organizational history for replication: the model that sustains later growth may address social needs and mobilize resources in ways founders did not initially anticipate.

title: From the Sovereign Debt Crisis to Pillar Two: The Changing Architecture of EU Tax Governance
affiliations: Masaryk University and Masaryk University

detail.title: From the Sovereign Debt Crisis to Pillar Two: The Changing Architecture of EU Tax Governance
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the structural transformation of EU tax governance from the Eurozone crisis to the implementation of the global minimum tax (Pillar Two). Combining historical institutionalism with tax law theories, we argue that traditional Westphalian tax sovereignty, protected by the unanimity rule, has become an illusion. Upon entering the Economic and Monetary Union, member states transitioned into currency users and consolidation states, thereby losing de facto fiscal autonomy. This evolution occurred through a failing forward logic across three phases. Phase I introduced coercive adjustment via Memoranda of Understanding. Phase II shifted toward incentivized sovereignty conditioned on structural reforms. Finally, Phase III institutionalizes pooled sovereignty as a safeguard against global tax competition and race to the bottom. To salvage democratic legitimacy and the tax social contract, national parliaments must actively reclaim the mandate for international tax coordination.

title: A Confidence-Dependent Core Framework for Integrated Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling, Lot-Sizing, Routing, and Inventory in Multi-Plant Supply Chains
affiliations: Payame Noor University

detail.title: A Confidence-Dependent Core Framework for Integrated Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling, Lot-Sizing, Routing, and Inventory in Multi-Plant Supply Chains
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the confidence-dependent Core (α-Core), a new solution concept for stochastic cooperative games, and applies it to integrated production-routing-inventory planning in multi-plant supply chains. The α-Core is defined as the set of imputations that are stable when the characteristic function is computed under a chance constraint with confidence level α. We prove three new theoretical results: (i) existence of a critical confidence level α* such that the α-Core is non-empty for all α ≥ α, (ii) monotonicity of the α-Core in α, and (iii) a sufficient condition for membership in the α-Core. The framework is applied to a two-stage stochastic program integrating flexible job-shop scheduling with sequence-dependent setup times, lot-sizing with setup carry-over and backlogging, vehicle routing, and inventory control. A simulation-optimization approach based on Enterprise Dynamics estimates stochastic parameters, and a hybrid MOSFS-Epsilon algorithm solves the second stage. A real pharmaceutical supply chain case study demonstrates a 14.2% cost reduction and a 9.8% delivery-time reduction. The critical confidence level is α = 0.87, providing a practical guideline: managers should set the confidence level at least 0.87 to ensure coalition stability.

title: KnowGuard: An Explainable, Outcome-Validated Decision-Support System for Knowledge-Concentration Risk Mitigation in Software Projects
affiliations: BRAC University

detail.title: KnowGuard: An Explainable, Outcome-Validated Decision-Support System for Knowledge-Concentration Risk Mitigation in Software Projects
detail.abstract: Knowledge concentration—the accumulation of project understanding in a small number of contributors—is a software engineering risk, yet existing tools measure it (e.g., truck factor and bus factor) rather than predict its consequences or prescribe mitigation. We present KnowGuard, an explainable decision-support system that (i) mines Git history alone, requiring no proprietary API access or issue-tracker integration, to identify Git-inferred contributor inactivity events (sustained commit-history gaps, not independently confirmed departures) and the post-inactivity disruption that followed; (ii) trains an interpretable gradient-boosted classifier using leakage-safe, pre-event features, including a co-change-graph-derived structural centrality signal adapted to this outcome-validated prediction task; and (iii) produces a ranked, SHAP-explained list of active contributors representing the highest disruption if their involvement were to end, together with the factors driving each score. This measures organizational dependency, not who will leave or individual value. Evaluated on 44 repositories, comprising 622 Git-inferred inactivity events with measurable outcomes after removing 33 bot accounts, KnowGuard achieves F1 = 0.674 (AUC = 0.731), outperforming naive commit-volume (F1 = 0.513) and truck-factor-membership (F1 = 0.214) baselines. The improvement is statistically significant (Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 0.0078 against both baselines across all eight cross-validation folds). Illustrative case studies provide face validity, not independent statistical evidence, by recovering well-known, verifiable maintainer transitions (e.g., Armin Ronacher from Flask, Guillermo Rauch from Socket.io, and Rich Harris from Rollup) using commit metadata, without being told their identities. We discuss limitations of Git-history-only signals and the domain gap between the open-source validation corpus and the enterprise context motivating the problem.

title: Numerical investigation of energy consumption by steadily traveling spherical particles in tube flow
affiliations: Manhattan University and Manhattan University

detail.title: Numerical investigation of energy consumption by steadily traveling spherical particles in tube flow
detail.abstract: The power required to drive a line of neutrally buoyant spherical particles moving along the centerline of a circular tube containing a flowing Newtonian fluid was investigated using ANSYS Fluent coupled with a Python script. The script automated the simulation process, enabling the present study to offer the most comprehensive investigation to date of this flow configuration. The study examined the effects of three key parameters: the sphere-to-tube diameter ratio (d/D), the sphere separation length-to-tube diameter ratio (L/D), and the Reynolds number (Re). Reynolds numbers were limited to Re≤100 to maintain stable axisymmetric flow conditions, although the full Navier–Stokes equations were solved throughout. Results showed that the relative apparent viscosity, μrel ; i.e., apparent viscosity relative to the actual fluid viscosity depends on d/D and L/D but is independent of Re over the range 0.1≤Re≤100. In addition, the ratio of sphere-to-mean-fluid velocity (Us/Uo) was found to depend primarily on d/D, with negligible dependence on Re and only a weak dependence on L/D. The simulations also revealed that the most energy-efficient method of transporting spherical particles through small tubes is to pack them as closely together as possible.

title: How Corner Is a Corner Case? Percentile Control for Highway Scenario Generation
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Wisconsin-Madison, University of Wisconsin-Madison and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: How Corner Is a Corner Case? Percentile Control for Highway Scenario Generation
detail.abstract: Generating corner-case scenarios with appropriate adversity in a simulation environment is critical for testing an autonomous vehicle (AV) software stack’s safety performance before deployment. Existing autonomous-driving scenario generators can enforce specific behavior, adversity, or feasibility conditions, but they provide limited control over how extreme a generated scenario is relative to plausible futures in the same traffic context. This study represents the adversity of a generated scenario as its percentile in the conditional distribution of future risk given the observed history. This view supports calibrated answers to two questions: how ”corner” a generated corner-case scenario is and how its ”cornerness” can be fine-tuned.To this end, we formulate history-conditioned risk-percentile requests and learn a reference risk distribution that maps each requested percentile to a physical risk target. We then use a percentile-conditioned joint diffusion model with sampling-time risk guidance to generate multi-agent futures, together with a reference-based criterion for evaluating percentile realization.Experiments use the minimum post-encroachment time (PET) between the ego and its surrounding vehicles as the risk surrogate on highD. On the primary evaluation set, our method realizes 1,422 of 1,440 requests within a 0.05 percentile tolerance (98.75%), with mean percentile error 0.00673 and PET-target error 0.00991 seconds. The resulting interface connects context-relative risk specification, physical realization, and evaluation through a common risk scale. Project website and videos of generated scenarios are available at https://hhjj233.github.io/CornerPercentile/.

title: Assessing Inter-regional Spillovers and Budget Optimization in Urban Energy Planning: A Case Study of Seoul's Green Transition

detail.title: Assessing Inter-regional Spillovers and Budget Optimization in Urban Energy Planning: A Case Study of Seoul's Green Transition

detail.abstract: As global urgency to mitigate climate change intensifies, cities have emerged as primary arenas for decarbonization. This study evaluates the economy-wide implications and fiscal viability of the 6th Seoul Regional Energy Plan (2025–2045) by integrating a Multi-Regional Input-Output (MRIO) model with a priority-based constrained optimization framework that enforces fiscal neutrality and sector-specific reallocation caps. Using the 2020 MRIO tables, we analyze the spatial spillovers of green investments across 17 South Korean regions and identify budget reallocation strategies that maximize macroeconomic benefits under strict fiscal neutrality. The results characterize Seoul's green transition as a national catalyst. While the building sector secures local employment, the transport and energy investments drive substantial regional spillovers, stimulating manufacturing growth in industrial belts. The optimization demonstrates that financing the plan entirely through internal budget reallocation, without external borrowing, yields a cumulative net macroeconomic output gain of +5,388 million USD over the planning period. This gain, however, is spatially uneven: almost the entire output benefit accrues outside Seoul, while Seoul itself records a net decline. The reallocation also produces a net employment loss of -70,286 person-years, concentrated in Seoul, as the defunded sectors, predominantly local construction and civil engineering, are more employment-intensive than the capital-intensive investment targets. The study thus shows that a self-financed municipal green transition can generate positive national output effects, while the spatial and employment trade-offs place much of the cost on the city that initiates it. The findings underscore the value of composition-oriented budget design and inter-regional coordination in scaling municipal climate investments.

title: A two-scale leakage model for cryogenic polymer seals: simulation and experimental validation

detail.title: A two-scale leakage model for cryogenic polymer seals: simulation and experimental validation

detail.abstract: Valve robustness and failure remain critical challenges in spacecraft engineering, particularly for valves operating with cryogenic media. To address this gap, this work introduces a multiscale model to predict leakage flow trends. The framework begins with a macroscopic valve simulation to determine the contact pressure between poppet and polymer seal seat. This pressure is applied on a small two-part unit cell (UC), where the length corresponds to the macroscopic contact length. From there, we analyze leakage flow between the contacting surfaces on the microscale. To account for the actual surface roughness, the UC surfaces are mapped using an optical 3D measurement system. The resulting interfacial leakage channels are identified by the Boykov-Kolmogorov algorithm to analytically determine the flow caused by a pressure difference. To predict future designs, a neural network was trained to estimate leakage based on the macroscopic setting, which is defined through material selection, temperature and pressure in operation, the system's tightening force and the geometric design of the seal seat. The model is calibrated based on test data of a baseline valve. Model verification is conducted using test data of a second valve which uses a similar tightening concept but features distinct design features and operational conditions. The comparison of the simulated results with the experimental results demonstrated a strong agreement across material variations, geometric designs and pressure levels, though the influence of temperature requires further investigation to fully resolve its impact on leakage trends.

title: Which Sensing Impacts the Decision? Sensor Tasking for Real-Time Bushfire Evacuation Operations
affiliations: Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University) - Department of Supply Chain and Logistics

detail.title: Which Sensing Impacts the Decision? Sensor Tasking for Real-Time Bushfire Evacuation Operations

affiliations.org_name: Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University) - Department of Supply Chain and Logistics

detail.abstract: Bushfire evacuation transport plans are committed on uncertain demand. Before warnings, pickups and shelter places are fixed, an incident team can task only a few sensing channels (aerial scans, mobility data, road counters, door-knock crews), each with a cost, latency and noise. We ask which sensing changes the decision. We formulate the problem as a partially observed Markov decision process whose terminal decision is a two-stage capacitated zone-to-pickup and shelter assignment, and rank observations by the decision regret they remove per unit of sensing cost, counting a signal only if it lands before the plan is due. On a separable subclass, variance-minimising sensing can capture no decision value, and with unit costs latency turns acquisition into deadline scheduling, where a greedy rule discarding late signals keeps at least half the attainable value. In a coupled experiment, ignoring landing times costs 9 to 23% in regret. In a 2019–20 East Gippsland hindcast with assumed shelter capacities and simulated sensing, three observations remove 99% of modelled provisioning regret out of sample, against 88% for variance sensing, and 66% against 58% when onesignal in four fails; with slack shelters no observation has value. Across 1,965 Victorian localities and 23 fire seasons, from pre-season data only, about 111 localities a season are in the balance; observing them at budgets of 10 and 20 lowers realised regret, mainly by avoiding warnings where fire did not arrive. The framework values a sensing stream by the transport plans it can change, not the uncertainty it removes.

title: Phase-Complete Seasonal Retiming of Published Airport Schedules under Uncertain Capacity-Window Starts
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Phase-Complete Seasonal Retiming of Published Airport Schedules under Uncertain Capacity-Window Starts

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Airport capacity declarations commonly report limits for 5-, 15-, and 60-minute windows, yet the start origin of an intermediate window may be absent from public machine-readable records. Because the same timetable can pass one partition and overload another, this omission creates a reproducibility and planning problem. This study develops an exact phase-complete seasonal retiming model that represents every distinct 15-minute partition induced on a five-minute schedule grid. A single recurrent-flight decision must remain feasible for all phase representatives, while a lexicographic objective first minimizes the number of retimed dated operations and then their absolute displacement. A constraint-separation procedure terminates with a full-model optimality certificate. The model is evaluated on 114,328 published LIVE movements over the same 154-day winter season at Congonhas and Recife, using airport-specific runway, directional, terminal, operating-hour, and closure declarations. Clock-aligned timetables require no repair. Phase-complete feasibility requires 475 retimed operations at Congonhas (0.584%; 3,020 operation-minutes) and 81 at Recife (0.245%; 535 operation-minutes). Congonhas responds mainly to total-movement concentration, whereas Recife responds only to directional concentration despite substantial hourly runway headroom. Requiring seasonally consistent decisions adds 118 movements at Congonhas relative to independent daily repair; carrier exposure caps add a further 28–48 movements and become infeasible at 0.5%. The results establish capacity-window origin as a decision-relevant declaration attribute and provide an open, auditable method for phase-robust schedule planning.

detail.abstract: Seismic site response analysis (SRA) is fundamental for geotechnical engineering and regional hazard assessment, yet the heavy computational cost of traditional physics-based solvers severely limits their application in large-scale stochastic simulations. While deep learning surrogates offer a promising alternative, current implementations frequently struggle with numerical dispersion and the "spectral bias" pathology when applied to highly stratified media. This study proposes a novel, high-fidelity Physics-Guided Neural Network (PgNN) surrogate specifically engineered for 1D seismic wave propagation. To accurately capture complex wave reflection and refraction mechanics, a Stochastic Bedrock Impedance Modeling strategy is introduced, assigning unique dynamic properties to the substratum of each profile. To ensure robust generalization, a deep architecture utilizing the C∞ continuous Swish activation function is trained on a massive database of 200,000 stochastic realizations, natively generated via a refined Thin Layer Method (TLM) to eliminate numerical aliasing, The framework demonstrates exceptional predictive reliability, yielding a global Coefficient of Determination (R²) of 0.9915 and effectively reconstructing full-spectrum amplification curves without spectral bias. To operationalize these findings, the PgNN is encapsulated into a standalone Graphical User Interface (GUI): the PgNN Unified Seismic Framework. This software provides near-instantaneous evaluation of key dynamic parameters, including the fundamental resonance frequency (f0) and peak spectral amplification (Amax). Building on these metrics, the study introduces a novel Dual-Criteria Site Classification Matrix-operationalized within the GUI— to bypass the conventional Vs,30 "blind spot"—a limitation recently acknowledged by next-generation European codes—by capturing the exact stratigraphic frequency signature. Furthermore, featuring a high-throughput stochastic module for regional seismic, the framework processes thousands of profiles in seconds to delineate data-driven "Resonance Avoidance Bands" (based on the 15th-85th percentile interval). This provides a transformative decision-support tool for urban planning and soil-structure resonance mitigation in alignment with seismic codes standards.

title: Charging-constrained fleet dispatching equilibrium in quota-regulated electrified ride-hailing markets: an aggregate game with endogenous charger queueing and nested-logit demand
affiliations: Harbin Industry University

detail.title: Charging-constrained fleet dispatching equilibrium in quota-regulated electrified ride-hailing markets: an aggregate game with endogenous charger queueing and nested-logit demand
detail.abstract: Electrified ride-hailing fleets in Chinese megacities operate under two constraints that conventional dispatching models treat separately, namely a municipal cap on the vehicles admitted to each administrative zone and a finite stock of fast-charging guns whose occupancy is determined by the dispatching decisions that platforms make. This paper develops an aggregate non-cooperative game in which competing platforms allocate an electrified fleet across zones, and in which the steady-state vehicle identity is extended so that the charging fleet is derived from zone-specific energy expenditure and an Erlang-C representation of the charger bank. Because the bank is shared, the dispatching decision of one platform raises the queueing delay experienced by its rival, adding a congestion externality to the matching externality that operates through waiting time, while travellers allocate latent demand between the platforms, the metro and the private car through a nested logit mechanism. Although the payoff is implicit and not globally concave, a restricted operating region is identified on which the augmented forward mapping is locally invertible and the payoff is concave, which yields a restricted generalized Nash equilibrium, and a variational characterization supplies a sufficient condition for uniqueness. A six-zone calibration of the Chengdu market shows that fleet-size asymmetry produces a zone-entry ladder whose thresholds are pushed upward by scarce charging capacity and higher tariffs, and that binding quotas convert part of the licensed fleet into idle capacity. Experiments covering charger density, energy prices, metro accessibility, quota tightening, entry and joint pricing indicate that the mechanism is robust.

detail.abstract: Public electric-vehicle charging infrastructure is planned over long investment horizons and must therefore remain robust to alternative pathways of electromobility development. This study proposes a stochastic macroscopic model for projecting the distribution of charger-side energy consumption per charging session, which is empirically applied and evaluated based on real-world data from public DC charging stations in the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The model-output session-energy distribution closely reproduces the observed distribution, especially in the case of the Czech Republic, where the dataset is more robust. Despite limitations related to data availability, charging-efficiency assumptions, and the relatively early stage of electromobility development in both markets, the proposed macroscopic model shows strong potential as a tool for forecasting the distribution of energy consumption per charging session under alternative future scenarios, owing to its transparent and parameterizable structure.

detail.abstract: Abelmoschus sagittifolius is a medicinal plant of increasing economic importance in Vietnam, yet information on its diseases remains limited. During field surveys in Hue, Vietnam, severe stem rot was observed on cultivated plants, with water-soaked, soft brown lesions that expanded rapidly and led to tissue maceration, wilting, and plant collapse under humid conditions. A fast-growing mucoralean fungus was consistently isolated from symptomatic stems. Morphological examination showed cottony to floccose colonies, broad hyaline coenocytic hyphae, and clustered sporangiola consistent with Choanephora spp. For molecular identification, the ITS and LSU rDNA regions were sequenced and analyzed using BLASTn, maximum-likelihood phylogeny, and Neighbor-Net split-network reconstruction. Analyses of the combined ITS-LSU dataset placed the two isolates within the Choanephora cucurbitarum clade, clearly separated from C. infundibulifera, and the network topology was congruent with the phylogenetic tree. In pathogenicity assays, inoculated A. sagittifolius plants developed typical stem rot symptoms within 10 days, whereas control plants remained symptomless. The same fungus was re-isolated from symptomatic inoculated tissues, fulfilling Koch’s postulates. Based on morphology, molecular phylogeny, split-network analysis, and pathogenicity tests, the causal agent of stem rot on A. sagittifolius was identified as C. cucurbitarum. This study represents the first documented report of this pathogen on A. sagittifolius in Vietnam and worldwide.

title: Robustness-Redundancy-Criticality Assessment for Pavement Network Vulnerability under Future Heat Stress
affiliations: Beijing University of Technology and Beijing University of Technology

detail.title: Robustness-Redundancy-Criticality Assessment for Pavement Network Vulnerability under Future Heat Stress
detail.abstract: The escalating temperatures driven by climate change are increasingly impacting infrastructure systems. This study develops a robustness-redundancy-criticality (B-R-C) framework to assess future heat-related vulnerability of the motorway network in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei (BTH) region using four CMIP6 climate models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. A heat exposure index integrating motorway mileage and annual heat days is proposed to characterize pavement heat exposure and shows a consistent relationship with rutting development. Pavement rutting increases progressively over the century, particularly after mid-century, leading to greater losses in robustness and redundancy under SSP5-8.5 than SSP2-4.5. By the end of the century, high-robustness and high-redundancy segments decrease from approximately 30% and 40% under SSP2-4.5 to 10% and 30% under SSP5-8.5, respectively. Network criticality is further quantified through travel-efficiency losses, and the resulting B-R-C framework supports maintenance prioritization and climate adaptation under limited resources.
